sections.mechanism_or_content: Section begins at the bottom of physical p.87 after the preceding proof; p.87 defines the discrete-time Dirichlet form and p.88 gives continuous-time/weighted-graph versions (3.76–3.77) and proves Lemma 3.24, the CT derivative identity for stationary-density L2 distance.

Theorem 3.25 states the centered-function Rayleigh–Ritz relaxation-time variational formula on p.89; pp.90–91 prove it by conjugating the reversible kernel to a symmetric matrix and applying the second-eigenvalue variational formula. The source notes the finite-state supremum is attained.

Lemma 3.26 is stated on p.91 and proved on p.92 by differentiating the squared L2 distance, applying the extremal characterization and integrating; Corollaries 3.27–3.28 on pp.92–93 compare collapsed chains and increased conductances.

Lemma 3.29 is stated and its direct edge/vertex-weight-ratio proof starts on p.93 and concludes on p.94; edge loops are excluded from extrema. The proof uses variational comparison, not path congestion.

Show relaxation time can change substantially after a small relative change in total edge weight: a single bridge versus a matching between cliques, and adding a clique among a sub-square-root number of new vertices. They motivate same-stationary-law comparison; they are not path constructions.

After Example 3.31 on p.94, Lemma 3.32 assumes the same stationary distribution and off-diagonal entrywise domination p_ij≥δp*_ij. Its conclusion follows from direct Dirichlet-form comparison. The following source remark proposes a residual-kernel mixture, but this Q need not be nonnegative under off-diagonal domination alone; full-entry domination suffices for that interpretation. This caveat does not invalidate the lemma and is not path routing.

Theorem 4.22 from §4.3.5 ends at the top of p.131; §4.4 starts on p.131. The source defines τ2=(1−λ2)^−1 in DT and λ2^−1 in CT, then Lemma 4.23 gives the CT τ2≤τ1≤τ2[1+½log(1/π*)] inequality and a separate DT τ1^(2) bound with factor 4e/(e−1).
